subject: ordered vector parameters & truncation vs. sorting

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: ordered vector parameters & truncation vs. sorting
parts:
Consider the following model(s), with and without the truncation:

transformed data {
int K;
K <- 10;
}
parameters {
real mu;
real<lower=0,upper=2> sigma;
ordered[K] y;
}
model {
mu ~ normal(0,1);
y[1] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
for (k in 2:K)
y[k] ~ normal(mu,sigma); // ??? T[y[k-1], ];
}

If we think about an ordered y as sampling a bunch of y values
and then sorting them, then I think we can skip the truncation.

If I think of generating the y one at a time, then I should
sample y[1] unconstrained, then sample y[2] with a lower bound of y[1], and
so on.

Running them in Stan, I get the following without truncation:

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y[1] -1.6 0.2 1.4 -4.6 -2.5 -1.5 -0.6 0.8 55 1
y[2] -1.0 0.1 1.2 -3.6 -1.8 -1.0 -0.2 1.3 69 1
y[3] -0.7 0.1 1.2 -3.2 -1.4 -0.6 0.1 1.4 129 1
y[4] -0.4 0.1 1.1 -2.7 -1.1 -0.4 0.4 1.7 198 1
y[5] -0.1 0.1 1.1 -2.2 -0.8 -0.1 0.5 2.0 365 1
y[6] 0.1 0.1 1.1 -2.0 -0.5 0.1 0.8 2.4 374 1
y[7] 0.4 0.1 1.1 -1.8 -0.3 0.4 1.1 2.8 392 1
y[8] 0.7 0.1 1.1 -1.6 -0.1 0.6 1.4 3.2 352 1
y[9] 1.1 0.1 1.2 -1.4 0.3 1.0 1.7 3.9 241 1
y[10] 1.6 0.1 1.5 -0.9 0.6 1.4 2.5 4.9 192 1

and the following with truncation:

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y[1] -0.1 0.1 1.6 -3.5 -1.2 -0.1 1.0 3.1 332 1
y[2] 0.9 0.1 1.6 -1.9 -0.3 0.8 1.9 4.2 203 1
y[3] 1.5 0.2 1.7 -1.5 0.4 1.5 2.6 5.0 123 1
y[4] 2.0 0.2 1.8 -1.2 0.7 2.0 3.2 5.9 94 1
y[5] 2.5 0.2 2.0 -1.1 1.0 2.4 3.7 6.6 86 1
y[6] 2.9 0.2 2.1 -1.1 1.4 2.9 4.3 7.1 83 1
y[7] 3.2 0.2 2.2 -1.1 1.6 3.2 4.8 7.5 82 1
y[8] 3.5 0.3 2.3 -1.0 1.9 3.6 5.1 7.9 80 1
y[9] 3.8 0.3 2.4 -1.0 2.2 3.9 5.5 8.4 78 1
y[10] 4.1 0.3 2.5 -0.9 2.4 4.1 5.9 8.9 75 1

The span of values in the truncated case is higher, and there's
a translation so that everything's relative to y[1], which has
a mean of 0.

I then compared a simple sorting model:

transformed data {
int K;
K <- 10;
}
parameters {
real mu;
real<lower=0,upper=2> sigma;
vector[K] y_raw;
}
model {
mu ~ normal(0,1);
y_raw ~ normal(mu,sigma);
}
generated quantities {
vector[K] y;
y <- sort_asc(y_raw);
}

which produces the result

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y[1] -1.6 0.2 1.4 -4.8 -2.4 -1.5 -0.7 0.7 83 1
y[2] -1.1 0.1 1.2 -3.6 -1.8 -1.0 -0.3 1.2 141 1
y[3] -0.7 0.1 1.1 -3.1 -1.4 -0.7 0.0 1.6 124 1
y[4] -0.4 0.1 1.1 -2.6 -1.1 -0.4 0.2 2.0 121 1
y[5] -0.2 0.1 1.1 -2.2 -0.9 -0.2 0.5 2.2 113 1
y[6] 0.1 0.1 1.1 -1.9 -0.7 0.0 0.7 2.4 105 1
y[7] 0.3 0.1 1.1 -1.5 -0.5 0.2 1.0 2.7 96 1
y[8] 0.6 0.1 1.2 -1.3 -0.3 0.5 1.4 3.0 87 1
y[9] 1.0 0.1 1.3 -1.1 0.0 0.8 1.8 3.8 79 1
y[10] 1.5 0.2 1.5 -0.9 0.4 1.4 2.5 4.8 71 1

and that looks to be within MCMC std error of the untruncated answer.
So this makes me think it's kosher to skip the truncation. Am I
out of my mind and is the untruncated version fundamentally flawed?

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: ordered vector parameters & truncation vs. sorting
parts:
On Wednesday, May 7, 2014 7:28:37 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
and that looks to be within MCMC std error of the untruncated answer.  
So this makes me think it's kosher to skip the truncation.  Am I
out of my mind and is the untruncated version fundamentally flawed?

In the untruncated case, the posterior distribution of y would be multivariate normal with a diagonal covariance matrix. But that is not what the planes of the distribution of y looks like in the sorted case


Ben
